definition: A table of tuples that all have the same attributes.
wrongs: A single column value stored in one cell.
A drawing of entities and diamonds used before tables exist.
A unit of work that commits or rolls back.
why: In the relational model, a relation is the set of tuples that share one schema.
example: A student table holds one row per student, and every row has id, name, and major.
scenario: A designer stores students as rows that all use the same columns, rather than as nested lists. What is that table in the relational model?
scenarioWhy: A relation is the table structure of tuples that share one set of attributes.

definition: One row of a relation, with a single value for each attribute.
wrongs: The set of legal values an attribute may hold.
The name and column list of a table, without the current rows.
A column that describes one property of every row.
why: Each tuple is one instance stored in the relation.
example: The student row (102, Ada, CS) is one complete record in the student table.
scenario: An import adds one student row containing an id, a name, and a major. What is that row called?
scenarioWhy: A tuple is a single row that supplies one value for every attribute of the relation.

definition: A named column of a relation that describes one property of each tuple.
wrongs: A complete row storing one value for every column.
A key that references a row in another table.
An auxiliary structure that speeds lookups.
why: The schema lists attributes, and every tuple provides one value for each of them.
example: In a course table, the credits column is a property recorded for every course row.
scenario: A course table has columns named code, title, and credits. What is the credits column called?
scenarioWhy: An attribute is a column, so credits names one property of each course tuple.

definition: The set of atomic values that an attribute is allowed to hold.
wrongs: The current rows stored in a table.
A foreign key linking two relations.
The physical order of rows on disk.
why: A domain constrains storage, for example integers for credits or strings for names.
example: The credits column accepts only integers from 1 to 6 and rejects other values.
scenario: A column must accept only integers from 1 to 6 and must reject the text six. What limits those legal values?
scenarioWhy: The domain is the set of legal atomic values for that attribute.

definition: The name, attributes, and constraints of a relation, separate from the rows stored at the moment.
wrongs: The rows that happen to be in the table right now.
A plan the optimizer chooses for one query.
A backup copy of the data files.
why: The schema is the design, while an instance is the data at a particular time.
example: Student(id, name, major) describes the table even when it currently contains no rows.
scenario: A catalog design lists table names and columns before any student has enrolled. What is that design called?
scenarioWhy: The schema describes structure and constraints, whether or not any rows have been inserted yet.

definition: The chosen candidate key that identifies each tuple and cannot be null.
wrongs: Any set of columns that is unique only because extra columns were added.
A column that points at a key in another table.
A key that may contain nulls as long as the other values differ.
why: One candidate key is selected as the primary key so every row has a unique, non-null identity.
example: student_id identifies each student row, and the table rejects a second row with the same id.
scenario: Every student row needs one unique, non-null identifier that other tables will reference. Which key should be designated?
scenarioWhy: The primary key is the unique, non-null identifier chosen for the table.

definition: A minimal set of attributes that uniquely identifies each tuple.
wrongs: A unique set that still contains attributes not needed for uniqueness.
A column that references another relation.
A non-unique column used only for sorting.
why: Removing any attribute from a candidate key would leave some tuples indistinguishable.
example: Both email and student_id uniquely identify a student, and neither needs an extra column.
scenario: Both national_id and email uniquely identify a person, and neither set has a spare column. What is each of those sets?
scenarioWhy: Each set is minimal and unique, so each one is a candidate key.

definition: A set of attributes that uniquely identifies tuples, even if it includes extra attributes.
wrongs: A minimal unique set with no attribute to spare.
A non-unique column that only describes a property.
A foreign key that may repeat.
why: Every candidate key is a superkey, but a superkey may contain attributes that uniqueness does not need.
example: The pair student_id and name still identifies each student because student_id alone is already unique.
scenario: student_id plus major still identifies each student, but major is unnecessary for uniqueness. What kind of key is that larger set?
scenarioWhy: The set is unique, but it is not minimal, so it is a superkey rather than a candidate key.

definition: An attribute set in one relation that must match a candidate key in another relation.
wrongs: The primary identifier chosen for the same table.
A check that a numeric column stays inside a range.
An index used only to speed a search.
why: Foreign keys are how rows in one table refer to rows in another.
example: enrolment.student_id must equal some student.student_id so every enrolment names a real student.
scenario: An enrolment row must point at a student row that already exists. Which key column expresses that link?
scenarioWrongs: A check constraint on a number
scenarioWhy: A foreign key requires the enrolment's student id to match an existing student key.

definition: A key formed by two or more attributes that together identify a tuple.
wrongs: A single system-generated number used as the only key column.
A foreign key that copies one parent column.
A non-key column determined by another non-key column.
why: No single attribute of the key is unique, but the combination is.
example: An enrolment table uses the pair student_id and course_id because one student takes many courses.
scenario: In an enrolment table, neither student_id nor course_id is unique alone, but the pair is unique. What is that key?
scenarioWrongs: A surrogate key of one column
scenarioWhy: The key needs both columns together, so it is composite.

definition: A distinguishable real-world thing represented in a conceptual database design.
wrongs: An association between two things, such as enrolment.
The set of legal values for one column.
A committed unit of database work.
why: Entity sets group instances of the same kind, and those sets are later mapped to relations.
example: In a university design, each student and each course is a thing the model must remember.
scenario: A university model must remember students, courses, and departments as the things of interest. What are those things called?
scenarioWhy: Students, courses, and departments are the entity sets in the conceptual model.

definition: An association among entities, such as a student enrolling in a course.
wrongs: A thing being modeled, such as a student or a course.
A column domain of allowed values.
A physical page of a data file.
why: Relationships record how entity instances are connected and may carry attributes of their own.
example: An enrols association links a student to a course and stores the term of that enrolment.
scenario: The design must record which students take which courses, not only the students and the courses. What should connect those sets?
scenarioWhy: A relationship associates student instances with the course instances they take.

definition: The number of entity instances allowed on each side of a relationship.
wrongs: The number of disk pages a table occupies.
The number of indexes defined on one column.
The isolation level of a transaction.
why: Ratios such as one-to-many state how many instances on each side may participate.
example: Each student has one department, while a department contains many students.
scenario: Each department has many students, and each student belongs to exactly one department. Which cardinality describes the department-to-student relationship?
scenarioWhy: One department relates to many students, so the department-to-student cardinality is one-to-many.

definition: An entity that cannot be uniquely identified without the key of an owner entity.
wrongs: An entity that has its own complete primary key.
A multivalued attribute drawn as a double oval.
A relationship with cardinality one-to-one.
why: Its primary key combines a partial key with the owner entity's key.
example: A dependent's name is unique only within one employee, so the dependent depends on the employee key.
scenario: A dependent cannot be identified by name alone and also needs the employee's id. What kind of entity is the dependent?
scenarioWhy: The dependent has no identity of its own and borrows the owner employee's key.

definition: A drawing of entities, attributes, and relationships used to design a database conceptually.
wrongs: A sequence diagram of method calls in a program.
A Gantt chart of project tasks.
A page table that maps virtual pages to frames.
why: The diagram communicates the conceptual schema before it is turned into tables.
example: A sketch shows a student rectangle and a course rectangle joined by an enrols diamond.
scenario: Before creating tables, a team sketches rectangles for students and a diamond for enrolment. What kind of diagram is that?
scenarioWhy: Rectangles for entities and diamonds for relationships are the notation of an ER diagram.

definition: The standard language for defining, querying, and changing data in a relational database.
wrongs: A markup language for web page structure.
A stylesheet language for visual layout.
A document format of nested name-value pairs.
why: SQL includes statements for schema definition, queries, updates, and access control.
example: A lab uses statements in this language to create a student table and then read students in one major.
scenario: An application must create tables and query rows in PostgreSQL using the standard relational language. Which language is that?
scenarioWhy: SQL is the language relational systems use both to define tables and to query them.

definition: An operation that keeps only the tuples that satisfy a condition.
wrongs: An operation that drops columns and keeps a subset of attributes.
An operation that combines every tuple of one relation with every tuple of another.
An operation that sorts a relation by one attribute.
why: Selection filters rows and corresponds to a WHERE condition in SQL.
example: Keeping only students whose major is CS discards every other student tuple.
scenario: A query must return only courses whose credits are greater than 3. Which relational-algebra operation filters those rows?
scenarioWhy: Selection keeps tuples that meet a predicate and drops the rest.

definition: An operation that keeps only the named attributes of a relation.
wrongs: An operation that keeps rows matching a condition.
An operation that matches tuples between two relations.
An operation that removes duplicate database servers.
why: Projection chooses columns, and in the formal algebra it also removes duplicate result tuples.
example: Asking only for name and major from a student table drops the id column from the result.
scenario: A query should return name and major, not every column of the student table. Which relational operation drops the other columns?
scenarioWhy: Projection retains the named attributes and discards the columns that were not requested.

definition: A join that returns only tuples whose join attributes match on both sides.
wrongs: A join that keeps every left tuple even when the right side has no match.
A join that keeps unmatched tuples from both sides.
A product that pairs every left tuple with every right tuple.
why: Tuples that fail the match condition are left out of the result.
example: Matching enrolments to courses on course id omits an enrolment whose course id is missing.
scenario: A report must list enrolments only when the course id exists in the course table. Which join keeps only those matches?
scenarioWhy: An inner join drops enrolments that have no matching course row.

definition: A join that keeps every tuple from the left relation and uses nulls when the right side does not match.
wrongs: A join that drops left tuples with no matching right tuple.
A join that keeps unmatched tuples from both relations.
A union that stacks two results with the same columns.
why: Unmatched left tuples remain visible so missing related data shows up as nulls.
example: Listing students together with enrolments still shows a student who has not enrolled in any course.
scenario: A student list must include students who have no enrolment, with nulls in the course columns. Which join does that?
scenarioWrongs: A right outer join from the enrolment side
scenarioWhy: A left outer join preserves every student and fills missing enrolment columns with null.

definition: A join that keeps unmatched tuples from both relations and fills the missing side with nulls.
wrongs: A join that keeps only tuples that match on both sides.
A join that keeps unmatched tuples from only the left relation.
A join that returns a row only when the right side matches.
why: Both left-only and right-only tuples survive, which an inner join would drop.
example: Combining departments and employees shows empty departments and also employees who have no department.
scenario: One result must show departments with no employees and employees with no department. Which join does that?
scenarioWhy: A full outer join retains unmatched rows from both the department side and the employee side.

definition: An SQL clause that gathers rows with equal values so aggregates can be computed for each group.
wrongs: A clause that sorts the final result.
A clause that filters individual rows before any grouping.
A clause that removes duplicate rows without computing aggregates.
why: Each distinct combination of grouping columns produces one group for functions such as COUNT.
example: Counting students while grouping by major returns one count for each major.
scenario: A registrar needs the number of students in each major, with one result row per major. Which clause forms those groups?
scenarioWhy: GROUP BY major builds one group per major so COUNT can be computed for each group.

definition: A clause that keeps or drops groups after aggregation, using a condition on each group.
wrongs: A clause that filters rows before they are placed into groups.
A clause that sorts groups alphabetically.
A clause that names the columns to display.
why: WHERE filters input rows, while this clause filters the groups produced by GROUP BY.
example: A condition that the student count exceeds 30 drops majors that are smaller than that.
scenario: After counting students per major, the query must drop groups whose count is 30 or less. Which clause filters the groups?
scenarioWhy: HAVING applies the count condition after groups exist, which is later than WHERE.

definition: A named query stored in the database and used like a table.
wrongs: A physical copy of a table stored only for backup.
An index that speeds searches on one column.
A procedure that runs automatically after an update.
why: Reading a view usually runs its defining query rather than fetching separately stored rows.
example: Analysts query a saved name that always means students whose status is active.
scenario: Analysts often need only active students, and the administrator wants them to query a saved name instead of repeating the filter. What should be created?
scenarioWhy: A view stores the active-student query under a name that can be selected like a table.

definition: An auxiliary structure that locates rows matching a search key without a full table scan.
wrongs: A saved query that presents a subset of rows.
A constraint that rejects a missing parent key.
A log of committed transactions.
why: The structure maps key values to row locations so the engine can read fewer pages.
example: A structure on the email column lets a login find one student without reading every student row.
scenario: Finding a user by email currently reads every row and is too slow. What should be added on the email column?
scenarioWhy: An index on email can point at the matching row without scanning the whole table.

definition: A balanced tree index whose sorted leaves support both equality and range searches.
wrongs: An unordered heap file of table rows.
A bitmap used only for low-cardinality columns in a data warehouse.
A hash structure that cannot efficiently serve a range of keys.
why: Leaf pages keep keys in order, so a range is a short walk along those leaves.
example: An index on order date finds every invoice dated between two days by scanning a sorted leaf range.
scenario: Queries often ask for invoices whose dates fall between two days, and the index should stay balanced. Which index structure fits?
scenarioWhy: A B+ tree keeps keys ordered in its leaves, so a date range is a contiguous leaf scan.

definition: An index whose key order matches the physical order of the table's rows.
wrongs: A secondary index that points at rows stored in a different order.
A full-text catalog of words inside documents.
A hash of the SQL text of a query.
why: Range scans on the clustering key read nearby rows together, and a table has only one such order.
example: A table stored in primary-key order keeps students with nearby ids on nearby pages.
scenario: Range scans on student_id should read nearby rows in key order, and the table can be stored in only one order. What kind of index matches that storage?
scenarioWrongs: A function index on a hash
scenarioWhy: A clustered index is the one order in which the rows themselves are stored.

definition: The rule that every attribute value is atomic and repeating groups are not allowed.
wrongs: The rule that every non-key column depends on the whole key.
The rule that non-key columns do not depend on other non-key columns.
The rule that every determinant is a candidate key.
why: A cell may not hold a list of values or a repeating group of the same fact.
example: Storing each phone number in its own row, instead of a comma-separated list in one cell, meets this rule.
scenario: One student cell contains two phone numbers separated by a comma. Which normal form requires that cell to hold a single atomic value?
scenarioWhy: A comma-separated list is not an atomic value, so the table is not in first normal form.

definition: The rule that every non-key attribute depends on the whole candidate key, not on part of it.
wrongs: The rule that forbids repeating groups in a cell.
The rule that removes a dependency between two non-key attributes.
The rule that every determinant must be a candidate key.
why: Partial dependencies appear when a composite key determines a column through only some of its attributes.
example: If enrolment is keyed by student id and course id, storing the student name there depends only on the student id.
scenario: A table keyed by student_id and course_id stores student_name, which depends only on student_id. Which normal form removes that partial dependency?
scenarioWhy: student_name depends on part of the composite key, which is a partial dependency forbidden by second normal form.

definition: The rule that every non-key attribute depends on the key rather than on another non-key attribute.
wrongs: The rule that each cell holds a single atomic value.
The rule that non-key attributes depend on all parts of a composite key.
The rule that eliminates multivalued dependencies.
why: Third normal form removes transitive dependencies in which a non-key column determines another column.
example: If a student row stores both department id and department name, the name depends on the department id.
scenario: Student stores dept_id and dept_name, and the name is determined by dept_id rather than by the student id. Which normal form removes that pattern?
scenarioWhy: dept_name depends on the non-key dept_id, a transitive dependency removed to reach third normal form.

definition: A normal form in which every determinant of a functional dependency is a candidate key.
wrongs: A form that only requires atomic attribute values.
A form that only removes partial dependencies on a composite key.
A form that only removes multivalued dependencies.
why: It catches some dependencies that third normal form still allows when a determinant is not a candidate key.
example: If room determines the course and room is not a candidate key, a timetable relation fails this stricter form.
scenario: In a timetable, room determines course and room is not a candidate key. Which normal form does that determinant violate?
scenarioWhy: Boyce-Codd normal form requires every determinant, including room, to be a candidate key.

definition: A constraint that each value of one attribute set corresponds to exactly one value of another.
wrongs: A dependency in which one attribute set corresponds to several independent values of another.
A rule that a foreign key matches a parent row.
A requirement that a transaction's writes are durable.
why: X determines Y when no two tuples agree on X and disagree on Y.
example: Each student id is stored with only one major, never with two different majors.
scenario: Each student id always appears with the same major. Which constraint describes that?
scenarioWhy: student_id determines major because one id never pairs with two majors.

definition: A dependency in which a key determines an attribute through some intermediate non-key attribute.
wrongs: A dependency on only part of a composite key.
A dependency in which a set of attributes determines itself.
A dependency that associates one value with several independent values.
why: If A determines B and B determines C, with B not a key, then C depends on A transitively.
example: Student id determines department id, and department id determines the department phone number.
scenario: Student id determines department id, and department id determines the department phone. What kind of dependency reaches that phone?
scenarioWhy: The phone depends on the student id only by way of the department id, so the dependency is transitive.

definition: Decomposing relations so each fact is stored once and update anomalies are reduced.
wrongs: Adding redundant columns so a query can avoid a join.
Building an index to speed a search key.
Writing a log record before a data page is updated.
why: Higher normal forms split tables so a change to one fact does not have to be repeated on many rows.
example: Moving a department phone out of every student row and into a department table stops repeating that phone.
scenario: A department phone is copied onto every student row, so one phone change needs many updates. What process moves that fact into its own table?
scenarioWhy: Normalization decomposes the table so the phone is stored once, with the department.

definition: A unit of database work that is applied completely or not at all.
wrongs: A saved query used like a table.
An index on a search key.
A single column constraint on legal values.
why: Its changes become visible together at commit, or they disappear if the transaction aborts.
example: Moving money debits one account and credits another as one unit of work.
scenario: A transfer must debit one account and credit another so both changes persist together or neither does. What should enclose those statements?
scenarioWhy: A transaction groups the debit and the credit into one success or one failure.

definition: The guarantee that every change in a transaction is applied, or none of them remain.
wrongs: The guarantee that concurrent transactions do not see one another's partial results.
The guarantee that committed data survives a crash.
The guarantee that a constraint true before the transaction is still true afterward.
why: If any step fails, recovery undoes the transaction so a partial update does not remain.
example: If crediting the destination account fails, the debit of the source account is undone as well.
scenario: A transfer debits an account and crashes before the credit. After recovery the debit is gone too. Which ACID property produced that outcome?
scenarioWhy: Atomicity rolls the whole transfer back when it cannot complete every step.

definition: The guarantee that a committed transaction leaves the database in a valid state.
wrongs: The guarantee that all steps of a transaction happen or none do.
The guarantee that committed writes survive a power failure.
The guarantee that one transaction cannot read another's uncommitted rows.
why: Integrity constraints that hold before the transaction still hold after it commits.
example: A completed money transfer still satisfies the rule that the sum of all balances is unchanged.
scenario: After a transfer commits, the sum of all account balances is the same as before. Which ACID property is that outcome?
scenarioWhy: Consistency means the committed transfer preserves the database's integrity rules.

definition: The guarantee that concurrent transactions do not observe one another's forbidden intermediate states.
wrongs: The guarantee that a transaction is all or nothing.
The guarantee that a commit survives a crash.
The guarantee that a foreign key points at an existing row.
why: Isolation levels specify which anomalies, such as dirty reads, concurrent transactions may allow.
example: Two transfers on one account each behave as if one finished before the other started.
scenario: Two clerks update the same account, and neither should see the other's uncommitted balance. Which ACID property requires that?
scenarioWhy: Isolation hides uncommitted work so concurrent clerks do not read each other's intermediate balances.

definition: The guarantee that changes from a committed transaction survive crashes and can be recovered.
wrongs: The guarantee that a transaction can be undone before it commits.
The guarantee that concurrent transactions are unaware of each other.
The guarantee that a transaction preserves integrity constraints.
why: After commit, the log can redo the changes even if memory contents are lost.
example: A ticket purchase that has committed is still recorded after the server loses power.
scenario: A booking commits, then the server loses power, and after restart the booking is still stored. Which ACID property explains that?
scenarioWhy: Durability requires a committed booking to remain available after a crash.

definition: The successful end of a transaction, after which its changes are permanent.
wrongs: The command that undoes a transaction that has not finished.
A marker inside a transaction that is not yet a permanent end.
A privilege that lets a user read a table.
why: Once it succeeds, the DBMS must be able to recover those changes and other transactions may see them.
example: Ending an order insertion successfully makes that order durable and visible to later queries.
scenario: Checkout has inserted the order and payment rows and now wants those changes to become permanent. Which command ends the transaction successfully?
scenarioWhy: COMMIT makes the inserted rows durable and ends the transaction successfully.

definition: The undoing of a transaction's uncommitted changes so they do not become permanent.
wrongs: The command that makes a transaction's changes permanent.
A command that deletes a table definition.
A command that grants a privilege to a user.
why: The log is used to restore the state from the start of the transaction or from a savepoint.
example: A clerk cancels a half-finished transfer, and the uncommitted debit disappears.
scenario: A clerk notices a mistaken debit before finishing the transaction and wants the prior committed state back. Which command does that?
scenarioWhy: ROLLBACK undoes the uncommitted debit and returns the database to the last commit.

definition: A rule that a transaction acquires all the locks it needs before it releases any lock.
wrongs: A distributed commit protocol with a prepare phase and a commit phase.
A logging rule that writes the log record before the data page.
A recovery step that writes dirty pages during a quiet point.
why: A growing phase followed by a shrinking phase keeps the schedule conflict serializable.
example: A transfer locks both accounts, updates them, and only afterward releases those locks.
scenario: The engine requires each transaction to finish acquiring locks before it unlocks anything. Which concurrency protocol is that?
scenarioWhy: Two-phase locking separates a growing phase of lock acquisition from a shrinking phase of releases.

definition: A cycle in which each transaction waits for a lock held by the next transaction.
wrongs: A read of data that another transaction later rolls back.
A repeated query that sees a newly inserted matching row.
A committed update that disappeared after a crash.
why: None of the transactions can proceed, so the system detects the cycle and aborts one of them.
example: One transfer holds account A and waits for B, while another holds B and waits for A.
scenario: T1 waits for a row lock held by T2, and T2 waits for a row lock held by T1. What is that wait cycle?
scenarioWhy: Each transaction waits for the other, forming a lock-wait cycle called a deadlock.

definition: A read of a value written by a transaction that has not committed.
wrongs: A repeated query that sees an extra row inserted by a committed transaction.
Two transactions writing the same item so one update disappears.
A read that cannot be repeated because a committed transaction changed the row.
why: If the writer later rolls back, the reader has used a value that never became permanent.
example: A report reads a new balance, and the transaction that wrote it then undoes that balance.
scenario: A report reads a balance written by another transaction that later aborts. Which anomaly occurred?
scenarioWhy: The report consumed an uncommitted balance that the writer subsequently rolled back.

definition: A repeated query that returns a different set of rows because another transaction inserted or deleted matching rows.
wrongs: A read of a value that is later rolled back by its writer.
Two writers each basing an update on the same old value.
A reread of one row that sees a new value in that same row.
why: The new or missing rows are phantoms; the first query did not lock the whole predicate.
example: A count of open seats changes because another transaction inserts a booking before the count is repeated.
scenario: A transaction rereads seats whose status is open and finds a new row committed by someone else. Which anomaly is that?
scenarioWhy: The new open-seat row is a phantom that was not in the first result set.

definition: The rule that every foreign-key value matches an existing parent key, unless nulls are allowed.
wrongs: The rule that a primary key is unique and not null.
The rule that a column's values belong to its domain.
The rule that a committed write survives a crash.
why: The DBMS rejects a child row that would point at a missing parent, and it controls deletes of parent rows.
example: Inserting an enrolment whose student id is not in the student table is rejected.
scenario: An enrolment insert uses a student id that does not exist, and the DBMS rejects the insert. Which rule caused the rejection?
scenarioWhy: The foreign key has no matching student, so referential integrity forbids the insert.

definition: A procedure the database runs automatically when a specified insert, update, or delete occurs.
wrongs: A named query that users select like a table.
A structure that speeds lookup by a key.
A number generator used for surrogate keys.
why: The procedure can enforce a rule or write an audit row without a separate statement from the application.
example: After an account balance changes, an automatic procedure writes the old and new balances to an audit table.
scenario: Every account update must write an audit row even when the application issues only the update. What database object does that?
scenarioWhy: A trigger on the update event runs the audit insert automatically.

definition: A named program stored in the database and invoked by clients with a call.
wrongs: A saved SELECT that is queried like a table.
A constraint that checks one column's range.
An index used to avoid a table scan.
why: The program runs on the server, close to the data, and many applications can call it.
example: Applications call one server routine that debits one account and credits another.
scenario: Several applications must run the same multi-statement transfer on the database server. What should hold that program?
scenarioWhy: A stored procedure keeps the transfer program in the database so every application can call it.

definition: The component that chooses an efficient execution plan for a SQL statement.
wrongs: The component that decides which transaction gets a lock.
The component that writes log records for recovery.
The component that chooses which memory page to evict.
why: It estimates the cost of scans, joins, and indexes, then picks a plan expected to be cheap.
example: For a login lookup, the planner uses an email index instead of reading every user row.
scenario: A SELECT could scan the whole table or use an index, and the engine picks the cheaper plan. Which component chooses?
scenarioWhy: The optimizer compares estimated costs and selects the plan used to run the statement.

definition: The techniques that let transactions run together without corrupting shared data.
wrongs: The choice of a cheap plan for one SQL statement.
The redo of committed work after a crash.
The replacement of buffer pages to free memory.
why: Locks, timestamps, or multiple versions coordinate conflicting reads and writes.
example: Row locks stop two transfers from updating the same account balance at the same moment.
scenario: Many tellers update accounts at the same time, and the DBMS must keep those updates from corrupting balances. What is that coordination called?
scenarioWhy: Concurrency control coordinates the tellers' transactions so conflicting updates stay correct.
